data.content_ref: inline:SRC_002's claim that resilience is a function of ignorance inherits its core uncertainty from a counterfactual known as the 'algorithmic convergence' problem: if all ostensibly independent operators in a decentralized network optimize using identical models or identical training data, their algorithms constitute an unobserved shared cause whose discovery would retroactively reveal that the failures were merely uncorrelated all along. The epistemic status of independence is therefore permanently hostage to the existence of such convergence, which the current foundation artifacts cannot detect without intervening on the shared training data itself. It is refuted if one can show that algorithmic convergence produces systematically divergent failure modes despite identical training data, breaking the shared-cause mechanism.
